Demonstrators had gathered Saturday near the Presidential Palace before violence erupted. In a statement released through his spokesperson, Ban condemned the bloodshed and on Sunday urged officials “to urgently initiate a fair process by which those responsible will be brought to justice.” He also said the “tragedy” resulted from a “lack of restraint on all sides.”

“The Secretary-General calls upon all concerned parties to resolve their differences through peaceful and democratic means and through the exercise of responsible leadership,” the statement said.

A police official reported that the number of people killed in Saturday’s unrest outside the Presidential Palace in Antananarivo, the capital, had climbed to 26. Officials said more than 80 others were hurt during the protest. The city was calm as mourners gathered for a public ceremony honoring those who died.

The confrontation grew out of a continuing power struggle over control of Madagascar’s government. Andry Rajoelina, the mayor of Antananarivo, had gone into the streets a week earlier and proclaimed himself leader of the Indian Ocean island nation. That followed a week of looting and violence that left at least 80 people dead and more than 300 injured.

President Marc Ravalomanana, however, dismissed Rajoelina from the mayor’s office and appointed another person to replace him.

Rajoelina organized Saturday’s rally at May 13th Plaza to present his proposed new government, according to Brittany Martin, an American citizen, Harvard Fellow and Antananarivo resident. Martin said the gathering was peaceful during the morning, but gunfire was heard in the afternoon after protesters moved from the plaza toward the palace. She said it was not clear where the shots originated.

Some news accounts attributed the gunfire to foreign mercenaries. Others said army guards were responsible, or that soldiers were firing at mercenaries in an effort to protect the crowd.

The unrest in Madagascar began January 26, when protesters entered state-controlled television and radio stations in Antananarivo. Earlier that day, the government had closed a radio station owned by Rajoelina. Weeks before, authorities had also shut down his television station after it broadcast an interview with former President Didier Ratsiraka.

Ravalomanana came to power in 2001 after forcing Ratsiraka out following a highly disputed and tense election. Ratsiraka later fled to France. Supporters of Ravalomanana have accused members of Ratsiraka’s family of encouraging the recent disturbances.

Public frustration has grown in Madagascar, where the World Bank says the average annual income is about $320. Reports that Ravalomanana recently purchased a $60 million airplane have added to the anger.

Rajoelina has called on his supporters to press for Ravalomanana’s resignation. He has said he intends to lead the country until a transitional government can be created in the nation, which lies off Africa’s southeastern coast.

Rodney Ford, a spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy, said the embassy had consistently encouraged talks. “What we’ve been pushing for is dialogue the whole time,” he said. Ford also said he had received reports that palace guards used tear gas and fired into the air in an attempt to scatter the protesters.

Journalist Dregoire Pourtier in Antananarivo, Madagascar, contributed to the report.

**Madagascar Protests: Deadly Palace Shooting Deepens Political Crisis**

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar —** Madagascar’s political crisis escalated sharply in early 2009 after security forces opened fire on opposition demonstrators near the presidential palace in the capital, killing dozens and intensifying a bitter power struggle between President **Marc Ravalomanana** and opposition leader **Andry Rajoelina**.

The unrest, which began as a dispute over governance, media freedom, and alleged abuse of power, developed into one of the most serious political confrontations in Madagascar’s recent history. Protests in the capital, Antananarivo, drew thousands of supporters of Rajoelina, the city’s former mayor, who accused Ravalomanana of authoritarian rule and mismanaging the country.

## Deaths Near the Presidential Palace

The most violent episode occurred on **February 7, 2009**, when opposition demonstrators marched toward the **Ambohitsorohitra presidential palace** in Antananarivo. The site was a sensitive government compound, and security forces had warned protesters not to approach.

As the crowd moved toward the palace, members of the presidential guard opened fire. Reports from the scene described panic as demonstrators fled amid gunfire. At least **28 people were reported killed**, though some accounts put the toll higher, and many more were wounded.

The shootings shocked the country and drew international condemnation. Opposition leaders accused the government of using lethal force against civilians, while government officials argued that protesters had attempted to seize a restricted state facility.

The deaths became a turning point in the crisis, hardening public opinion against Ravalomanana among many opposition supporters and increasing pressure on his administration.

## Rajoelina vs. Ravalomanana

The confrontation centered on the rivalry between **Andry Rajoelina**, a former disc jockey and media entrepreneur who became mayor of Antananarivo, and **Marc Ravalomanana**, a wealthy businessman and two-term president.

Rajoelina had built a political following by criticizing what he described as Ravalomanana’s concentration of power and alleged conflicts of interest between the presidency and the president’s business empire. The dispute worsened after the government shut down Rajoelina’s television station, **Viva TV**, in late 2008 after it broadcast an interview with former president Didier Ratsiraka, who was living in exile.

Rajoelina framed the shutdown as an attack on press freedom and used it to rally opposition supporters. In January 2009, protests turned violent, with looting and fires reported in Antananarivo and other cities. Rajoelina later declared that Ravalomanana was no longer fit to govern and called for a transitional authority.

Ravalomanana rejected the challenge, insisting he remained the legitimate elected president. His government dismissed Rajoelina’s movement as an unconstitutional attempt to seize power.

The crisis continued to deepen after the palace shooting. Sections of the military became increasingly reluctant to enforce orders against protesters, and divisions within the armed forces undermined Ravalomanana’s position. In March 2009, Ravalomanana resigned under mounting pressure and transferred authority to a military directorate, which quickly handed power to Rajoelina. Rajoelina then became head of a transitional government, a move widely viewed internationally as unconstitutional.

## U.N. and International Response

The **United Nations** urged restraint throughout the crisis and called for dialogue between the rival sides. U.N. officials expressed concern over the loss of life and warned that continued violence could further destabilize Madagascar.

Then-U.N. Secretary-General **Ban Ki-moon** appealed for calm and encouraged a peaceful, negotiated solution. The United Nations, along with the **African Union**, the **Southern African Development Community (SADC)**, and other international partners, supported mediation efforts aimed at ending the standoff and restoring constitutional order.

Following Rajoelina’s assumption of power, the African Union suspended Madagascar, calling the transfer of power unconstitutional. International donors also reviewed or suspended portions of assistance, adding economic pressure to an already fragile country.

The U.N. continued to back negotiations for a transition process and eventual elections. The crisis left Madagascar diplomatically isolated for years, and the country did not fully return to constitutional order until later elections were held.

## Lasting Impact

The 2009 protests and the killings near the presidential palace marked a defining moment in Madagascar’s political history. The violence exposed deep dissatisfaction with Ravalomanana’s rule but also led to a controversial transfer of power that many foreign governments and regional organizations rejected as a coup.

The crisis damaged Madagascar’s economy, weakened public institutions, and disrupted international aid. It also underscored the recurring instability that has shaped the island nation’s politics since independence.

For many Malagasy citizens, the February 2009 palace shootings remain a symbol of the high human cost of political confrontation and the dangers of unresolved disputes between elected leaders, opposition movements, and the security forces.

The killings drew concern from diplomats and regional observers, who urged restraint and called for dialogue between the rival camps. The deadly rally has left Madagascar at a dangerous crossroads, with Rajoelina demanding political change and Ravalomanana refusing to yield to pressure from the streets. The crisis has drawn growing concern from the international community. Regional organizations, diplomats, and religious leaders have urged both sides to step back from confrontation and enter peaceful dialogue. Calls for mediation have intensified, with church leaders and civil society groups offering to help facilitate talks between the presidency and the opposition.

International partners have emphasized that Madagascar’s political crisis must be resolved without violence and within a democratic framework. They have warned that prolonged instability could harm the country’s economy, deter investment, disrupt tourism, and worsen hardship for ordinary citizens.

Madagascar, one of the world’s poorest countries despite its rich biodiversity and natural resources, remains highly vulnerable to political and economic shocks. Many citizens already face unemployment, food insecurity, and limited access to public services. Analysts warn that continued unrest could deepen social divisions and weaken state institutions.

For now, both Rajoelina and Ravalomanana appear under pressure from their supporters not to back down. Rajoelina has continued to position himself as the voice of popular opposition, while Ravalomanana has insisted on defending his mandate as president.

The central challenge remains whether the two rivals can move from confrontation to negotiation. Religious leaders, civic groups, and foreign diplomats have urged both camps to avoid inflammatory rhetoric, condemn violence, and engage in meaningful talks.

As demonstrations continue, Madagascar stands at a critical political crossroads. The outcome will depend not only on the actions of Rajoelina and Ravalomanana, but also on whether national institutions, civil society, and international mediators can help steer the country toward a peaceful resolution rather than a deeper crisis.
